register.name: Heat wave
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in a ten-year stretch around 2050 (about 14 times a year).

sub_causes.name: A blackout during a heat wave
sub_causes.note: When the power fails in extreme heat, air conditioning fails for everyone at once. It is the most dangerous combination; where it matters most it is a named scenario.

register.name: Dust storm
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will be caught in a dust storm that closes roads or fouls the air at home in the next ten years.

register.name: Medical emergency
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 99 will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Far from emergency care
sub_causes.note: Ambulances take about twice as long to reach rural homes (a median of about 14 minutes against 7).

sub_causes.name: Falls
sub_causes.note: Falls are a leading reason older adults need emergency care; clear floors and light the way at night.

register.name: Strong wind
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 98 (68 to nearly all) will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Derecho
sub_causes.note: A fast line of storms with hurricane-force gusts over hundreds of miles; outages can last days. Counted in the windstorm rate.

register.name: Phone or internet outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will lose phone and internet service for hours in a network outage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: GPS or radio disruption
sub_causes.note: Space weather or jamming can degrade navigation and timing. Keep a paper map for the way home.

register.name: Supply chain disruption
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Fuel shortage
sub_causes.note: Gas stations run dry for days (the Colonial Pipeline shutdown, May 2021, and before hurricanes). It matters most with a generator or a long drive.

sub_causes.name: Cut off: an island or a single road
sub_causes.note: A bridge, ferry or the only road closes and the community is cut off for days. Plan for longer if that is you.

register.name: Local water or gas outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (50–95) will have a water main break or boil-water notice in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Toxic algae in the water supply
sub_causes.note: Algae toxins reach the treatment plant and a do-not-drink order follows (Toledo, 2014). Counted in the water-notice rate.

sub_causes.name: Gas main over-pressure or leak
sub_causes.note: Gas mains over-pressure or leak and homes must be evacuated (Merrimack Valley, 2018). If you smell gas, leave first, then call.

sub_causes.name: Water system failure for weeks
sub_causes.note: A treatment plant or system fails for weeks (Jackson, Mississippi, 2022; Asheville, 2024). The water targets use the county's drinking-water violations to size it.

sub_causes.name: Sewer failure
sub_causes.note: Pumps stop or mains break and toilets cannot be flushed. The sanitation supplies follow the water target.

register.name: Stranded in a vehicle
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (39–98) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Black ice or dense fog
sub_causes.note: Chain-reaction crashes and closed highways. Counted in the stranding rate.

sub_causes.name: Transit shutdown or strike
sub_causes.note: Buses and trains stop and commuters without a car are stuck. Counted for commuters who travel by transit.

register.name: Job loss
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 77 (64–91) will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Livestock or poultry disease
sub_causes.note: An animal-disease outbreak (bird flu in dairy or poultry) can hit a farm's income.

sub_causes.name: Recession layoffs
sub_causes.note: Layoffs cluster in downturns; the high end of the job-loss range is a recession year.

register.name: Eviction
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 40 (28–59) will be taken to court and ordered to leave their rented home in the next ten years.

register.name: Medicine shortage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 39 (18–78) will have a daily medicine they cannot fill for days or weeks because of a shortage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Hospital supply shock
sub_causes.note: A key hospital supply runs short (IV fluids in 2024, after Hurricane Helene closed a plant that makes a large share of the country's supply) and planned care is delayed.

register.name: Chemical spill or release
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 30 (10–59) will be told not to drink the tap water, or to stay inside, after a chemical spill in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Release from a chemical plant
sub_causes.note: A plant that uses large amounts of toxic or flammable chemicals has a release or explosion (West, Texas, 2013). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

sub_causes.name: Train derailment with chemicals
sub_causes.note: A train carrying chemicals derails and burns or leaks; homes within a mile or two are evacuated (East Palestine, 2023).

sub_causes.name: Tanker truck spill
sub_causes.note: A tanker crash closes roads and may bring an order to stay inside nearby.

sub_causes.name: Pipeline rupture
sub_causes.note: A gas or oil transmission pipeline ruptures and burns or spills; nearby homes are evacuated.

sub_causes.name: Refinery, tank farm or port fire
sub_causes.note: A large industrial fire brings orders to stay inside and smoke for days.

sub_causes.name: Chemical spill into the water supply
sub_causes.note: A spill upstream of a water intake brings a do-not-use order for days (Elk River, West Virginia, 2014). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

register.name: Civil unrest
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 26 (10–45) will live under a curfew because of unrest in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Unrest around elections
sub_causes.note: Protests, clashes or curfews around elections or political events.

register.name: Cyberattack on services
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (7–39) will lose pharmacy, payment or other services to a computer outage or cyberattack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Critical software failure
sub_causes.note: A faulty update or cloud outage takes down hospital, airline, bank or 911 systems for a day or more (July 2024). Counted in this rate.

sub_causes.name: Card or bank payment outage
sub_causes.note: Cards, bank apps or cash machines stop for hours to days. Keep some cash in small bills.

register.name: A household member is arrested or detained
register.frequency_sentence: For households with people the ages of yours, about 2 in 100 have someone arrested in a year, going by what people tell a national survey (2022–2024); police records suggest up to about 4 in 100. People arrested once are often arrested again, so over ten years fewer households are affected than a year-by-year count suggests. This counts arrests, not guilt or convictions.

register.name: Burst pipe or water leak
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (7–16) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Sewer backup
sub_causes.note: Sewage backs up through basement drains; standard home policies leave it out unless you add sewer-backup cover.

register.name: Pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (3–23) will live through a pandemic that changes daily life in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Mosquito- or tick-borne outbreak
sub_causes.note: Local dengue or West Nile spread brings spraying and advisories.

sub_causes.name: Local disease outbreak
sub_causes.note: Measles, hepatitis A or Legionnaires' in the community keeps people out of school or work. Check your vaccinations.

sub_causes.name: Bird flu (H5N1)
sub_causes.note: A candidate pandemic strain that so far passes from animals to people, not between people.

register.name: Long illness in the household
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–26) will have someone sick at home for weeks in the next ten years.

register.name: Break-in
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–18) will have a break-in in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Identity theft and disaster scams
sub_causes.note: Accounts opened in your name, or fake contractors and FEMA impostors after a disaster. A credit freeze is free.

register.name: Death or disability of an earner
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 9 (5–14) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Death in the family
sub_causes.note: A family member who does not earn dies: funeral costs and time off work.

register.name: Winter storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 8 (3–23) will be snowed in or lose power in a winter storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Blizzard or lake-effect snow
sub_causes.note: Whiteouts or very deep snow close roads for days. Counted in the winter-storm rate.

sub_causes.name: Roof damage under snow
sub_causes.note: Heavy snow or ice loads a roof until it sags or fails. Counted in the winter-storm rate; clear flat roofs early.

register.name: Drought
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 8 (2–35) will face water limits in a drought in a ten-year stretch around 2050.

register.name: Hurricane
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 6 (3–11) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in a ten-year stretch around 2050.

sub_causes.name: Inland flooding from a tropical storm
sub_causes.note: A weakening hurricane can drop a foot or more of rain far inland (Helene in western North Carolina, 2024), cutting water service for weeks.

register.name: House fire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a house fire, in their home or next door in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
sub_causes.note: Carbon monoxide from a furnace, generator or car builds up indoors, most often after storms when generators run too close to the house. Shown beside fires, not added to them; a CO alarm is the defence.

sub_causes.name: Lithium battery fire
sub_causes.note: E-bike, scooter and power-bank batteries can catch fire while charging; charge them where you can see them.

register.name: Regional blackout
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (1–14) will lose power in a regional blackout that is not caused by weather in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Attack on power substations
sub_causes.note: Gunfire or sabotage at substations can cut power to a county for days (Moore County, North Carolina, 2022). Utilities report about 78 cases of attack, vandalism or theft a year, most with no outage (2019–2023).

sub_causes.name: Cyberattack on the grid
sub_causes.note: Hackers switched off parts of Ukraine's grid in 2015; no US case has cut power. Utilities report about 7 cyber events a year (2019–2023).

register.name: Wildfire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–17) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in a ten-year stretch around 2050.

register.name: Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (fewer than 1 to 5) will be cut off or lose building services in a flood in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Flash flood
sub_causes.note: Water rises in minutes on roads and near creeks; most flood deaths are people driving into it. Counted in the flood rate; turn around, don't drown.

sub_causes.name: Basement or street flooding in heavy rain
sub_causes.note: Drains overflow and water or sewage comes up into basements outside the mapped flood zone. It is the outside-the-zone part of the flood rate, higher with a basement.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Counted on the dam and levee card, not here: leveed land is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone.

register.name: Lightning
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (fewer than 1 to 6) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.

register.name: Hail
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 2) will have hail damage their home or car in the next ten years.

register.name: Attack or threat closes your area
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 710 and 1 in 45 households like yours would have an attack or threat close their area or its transit for half a day or more in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler, AZ urban area is one of the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, chosen by the risk the Department of Homeland Security assigns them. It gets about 2 in 100 of the money, which is how this estimate weighs your area.

register.name: Dam or levee failure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 3,200 and 1 in 160 households like yours would be told to leave because a dam or levee fails or threatens to in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Land behind a levee is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone, so the flood card does not count it; a levee that is overtopped or breaks floods it deep and fast. Counted here.

sub_causes.name: Mine tailings or coal slurry dam failure
sub_causes.note: A mining-waste dam fails and sends slurry downstream. Counted with the other dams in the inventory.

location_factor.label: No high-hazard dam within 10 km lists your ZIP code's towns as the place a failure would flood. About 6.3 in 100 people in Maricopa County live behind a levee.

register.name: Earthquake
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 1,200 households like yours will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Liquefaction
sub_causes.note: Wet, sandy ground turns to slurry in strong shaking; pipes and foundations fail. Water outages last longer where it happens.

sub_causes.name: Fire after an earthquake
sub_causes.note: Broken gas lines and low water pressure let fires spread after a big earthquake. Know how to shut off the gas, and leave it to the gas company to turn it back on.

register.name: Tornado
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 1,700 (1 in 5,600 to 1 in 490) households like yours will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.

register.name: Nuclear power plant accident
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 2,000 (1 in 10,000 to 1 in 500) households like yours will be told to stay inside or leave after a nuclear power plant accident in the next ten years.

register.name: War with attacks on US infrastructure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 250 and 1 in 13 households like yours would lose power, water or phone service for days to attacks in a war in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county has military sites, a big city, a port or a refinery nearby: the kinds of places attacks on infrastructure aim at.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a winter storm (about 8 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Outages of power, water or phones for days, and shortages across the country.

register.name: Financial crisis with bank closures
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 11 households like yours would have banks close for three days or more in a financial crisis in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Your own bank fails
sub_causes.note: Insured deposits (up to $250,000 per person at each bank) move to another bank, usually within days. The FDIC counts about 23 failures a year (2001–2025), most of them small banks.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a pandemic that changes daily life (about 11 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Cards and bank transfers stop for days.
register.what_it_changes: Keep some cash in small bills (already in your plan) and a second account at another bank (free).

register.name: Very large volcanic eruption
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 130 and 1 in 26 households like yours would live through a year or two of higher food prices after a very large eruption somewhere in the world in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A Yellowstone super-eruption
sub_causes.note: Devastation nearby and ash across much of the country. The USGS puts it at about 1 in 730,000 a year.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: A year or two of higher food prices and some shortages.

register.name: Severe pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 21 households like yours would live through a pandemic far deadlier than COVID-19 in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A natural pandemic as deadly as 1918
sub_causes.note: The 1918 flu killed about 675,000 Americans. Records of pandemics over four centuries give the chance.

sub_causes.name: An engineered germ
sub_causes.note: A germ made or changed on purpose. There is no record to count; it is part of the expert range.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a house fire (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Months of disruption, strained hospitals and lost income.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing new: the pandemic row already sizes your food and medicine.

register.name: Nuclear attack or EMP
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 3,300 and 1 in 28 households like yours would be in a blast zone or under dangerous fallout in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Limited strike on US territory
sub_causes.note: One or a few weapons on US soil, for example a strike on Guam, Hawaii, Alaska or a West Coast base. It adds to your chance only where your county is a plausible target.

sub_causes.name: A crude nuclear device in a city
sub_causes.note: Heavy damage within about a mile, and everyone within 50 miles told to get inside. It adds to your chance by your metro area's share of FEMA's terrorism-preparedness money.

sub_causes.name: Electromagnetic pulse (EMP) from a high-altitude burst
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack: a burst high above the country could damage electronics and black out a region. EPRI's 2019 study found little damage to large transformers and did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months. The claim that most Americans would die rests on testimony that assumed such a blackout for a year, not on a published model.

sub_causes.name: Disruption across the country
sub_causes.note: Shortages, power cuts and lost income even far from any target. Shown for everyone and never added to your local chance.

sub_causes.name: A nuclear weapon used elsewhere in the world
sub_causes.note: At home: market shocks, shortages and worry, with no fallout of concern. Never added to your local chance.

location_factor.label: You live in the Phoenix metro area. Because of its size and importance, a place like this is treated as a likely target in a large nuclear war. That does not mean an attack is likely, only that the danger here would be greater than in most places.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Life-threatening: blast or heavy fallout near likely targets.
register.what_it_changes: One free step: pick your shelter spot at home and at work (a basement, or the middle of the building away from windows).

register.name: Severe solar storm
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 7,600 and 1 in 150 households like yours would lose power for days to a severe solar storm in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county is at a low geomagnetic latitude (about 40°). Solar storms drive the strongest currents into long power lines nearer the magnetic pole, so the chance of a long outage here is about 0.44 of the national average. The ground's conductivity also matters and is not counted.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than hail damage (about 1 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Power out for days, and longer where large transformers fail.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your power plan: a solar storm harms long power lines, not phones or radios.

register.name: Power out for months (any cause)
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 22,000 and 1 in 49 households like yours would be without power for two months or more in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A severe solar storm
sub_causes.note: Long outages where large transformers fail; most places would be back within days.

sub_causes.name: EMP from a nuclear attack
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack; EPRI's 2019 study did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months.

sub_causes.name: Attacks on the grid in a war
sub_causes.note: Cyberattacks, sabotage or missiles on power plants and lines.

sub_causes.name: Your county's own outage record
sub_causes.note: Storms and failures like the ones in your county's outage records, with the long tail the records cannot show yet.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a wildfire (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: No power for months: water, heat, medicine and money all affected. Puerto Rico waited 328 days after Hurricane Maria.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to stockpile for months. What helps instead: a way to treat water from a nearby source, a way to cook without power, a plan for toilets and waste, and some cash.

register.name: Chemical, biological or radiological attack
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 51,000 and 1 in 250 households like yours would be told to stay inside, or to collect medicine at a public site, after a chemical, biological or radiological attack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Chemical
sub_causes.note: A toxic chemical released on purpose: shelter inside for hours, or leave the immediate area if told to.

sub_causes.name: Biological
sub_causes.note: A germ spread on purpose (the anthrax letters of 2001): stay home, and collect preventive medicine at a public site if told to.

sub_causes.name: Radiological ("dirty bomb")
sub_causes.note: Shelter inside for hours; the area may stay closed for weeks.

location_factor.label: The Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler, AZ urban area is one of the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, chosen by the risk the Department of Homeland Security assigns them. It gets about 2 in 100 of the money, which is how this estimate weighs your area.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than an attack or threat closing your area (about 6 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: An order to stay inside for hours, closed buildings, or medicine handed out at public sites.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your basics: your three-day supplies cover sheltering inside.

register.name: Mass shooting or bombing
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 1,000,000 and 1 in 100,000 households like yours would have someone hurt in a mass shooting or bombing in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The data are too sparse to say where this is more likely, so the chance is the same everywhere.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a nuclear plant accident (about 1 in 2,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to buy. Two free steps: know "run, hide, fight", and learn to stop bleeding.

This number mostly depends on how often pandemics happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long times without shopping from store shortages and runs on stores last (expert estimate).

buckets.name: Dangerous heat or cold indoors

buckets.name: Medication and medical-supply continuity

This number mostly depends on how long gaps in medicine from a shortage of a daily prescription last (expert estimate) and how often medicine shortages happen where you live (expert estimate).

buckets.name: No phone, internet or card payments
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 45 (20–90) will lose phone, internet or card payments for a day or more in the next 10 years.

This number mostly depends on how often windstorms happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long phone and payment outages from short storm outages last (expert estimate).

frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (80–100) will have someone stranded away from home at least once in the next 10 years.

The get-home bag is sized by the walk home at about 3 miles an hour, with about half a litre of water per hour in hot weather.

buckets.name: Medical emergency when help is slow
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, nearly all (95 or more) will have a medical emergency at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: House fire
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a home fire at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Home and personal security
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 35 (20–50) will have a break-in or a nearby curfew at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Unhealthy air indoors

requirements.plain: Backup power for medical equipment: a CPAP uses about 170 Wh a night with the humidifier on (about 96 with it off). That is about 170 Wh a day × 3 days = 510 Wh. Keep spare batteries charged, and ask your utility about its list for customers who need power for medical equipment. (SIL, Ready.gov)
1 spare battery for each powered medical device: ask the maker which battery fits and how long it runs, and keep it charged. (Ready.gov, SIL)
1 battery light: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

A way to recharge from the car, because a medical device's battery needs topping up every day the power is out: a 12-volt charger, or a small inverter (about 150 W) for chargers that plug into the wall. It tops up phones, power banks, rechargeable lights and a power station. Run the engine only outdoors, never in a garage, even with the door open (CDC). Check that the inverter's watts cover the medical device's charger (see its label). (Oregon OEM, CDC, SIL; some amounts are estimates)

1 pair of appliance thermometers, one in the fridge and one in the freezer: after a power cut, keep refrigerated food only if it stayed at 40 °F or below, and throw out perishable food that was above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. (Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) to run the medical equipment through the outage. Your essential load (medical equipment and phones) is about 185 Wh a day, 560 Wh for 3 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 4.9 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. (SIL, retail prices, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 3 days = 2,990 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

For a boil-water notice of up to 5 days: make about 1.5 gallons of drinking water safe each day, about 7.5 gallons in all. To make it safe, boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. A gas stove can boil water while the gas flows; never use a camp stove or grill indoors. (Ready.gov, CDC, NCA5 Atlas, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

If you boil on a camp stove outdoors, about 1 lb of propane brings 28 L to a boil (about 25 to 30 L a pound). Never use a camp stove indoors, and keep no more than 2 one-pound cylinders inside. (EIA, local fire code, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 person × 1.75 gallons a day × 5 days = 8.8 gallons. Your county has at least 30 days a year at 95 °F or more, and drinking water can double in heat, so each person gets 1.75 gallons a day. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. (Ready.gov, CDC, NCA5 Atlas; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 1 person × 5 days = 3 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 1 person × 5 days = 5 cups, about 0.3 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

1 adult at about 2,262 kcal a day: about 2,262 kcal a day × 10 days = 22,600 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $101 for 10 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 20 % for a household of 1). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $25 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $271 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $102 to $441). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,262 kcal a day) one lasts about 17 to 23 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

Fuel for a camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 1 person × 10 days = 2 lb, or 4 butane canisters of 0.5 lb each. Use it outdoors only, never indoors (carbon monoxide), and store it cool, away from heat. (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 1 person × 10 days = 2 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 1 person-month: 1 person × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 450 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 1 person aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 1 cycle's worth, about 20 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: 1 battery fan: 1 for the home. In a county as hot as yours a home without power soon passes 90 °F, and above that a fan stops helping, so fans do not count toward your heat plan: the place you would go does. In a study of three US cities, a blackout of several days during a heat wave more than doubled the expected heat deaths. (CDC, NCA5 Atlas, Stone et al.; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: 1 cooling towel, one for each person, to wet and wear on the neck. In a county as hot as yours they help, but they do not replace going somewhere cooler. (NCA5 Atlas; some amounts are estimates)

A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. In a county as hot as yours this plan is your heat cover: write down "If the power is off and it is 90 °F inside, we go to ___" (a cooling centre, or a relative or friend with power), and how you will get there. (CDC, Ready.gov, NCA5 Atlas; some amounts are estimates)
1 room thermometer in the room where the most vulnerable person sleeps: fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors, so when it reads higher, go somewhere cooler. (CDC)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 21 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. For medicine the plan keeps at most a month on hand: agencies advise 7 days to two weeks (Red Cross, CDC, Florida), and a longer target is kept up with 60- to 90-day fills from your drug plan (Medicare). (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 1 phone × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 3 days without power = 50 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 written contact card, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $120: half of 3 days of your usual spending ($2,600 a month), the part that goes on food, fuel and medicine. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

1 go-bag, one for each person: a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents on paper and on a flash drive, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, an old pair of prescription glasses, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 2 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 1.8 gallons a day for the 1 person × 2 days = 3.5 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 2,262 kcal a day × 2 days = 4,500 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)
Keep the vehicle at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. (Ready.gov)

Person 1 travels 8.7 miles (14 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 2.9 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 1's walk home: 2.9 hours × about 0.71 L an hour in heat = 2.1 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, NIOSH; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 300 kcal for 2.9 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

1 car emergency kit: jumper cables or a charged jump pack you have tried, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks, and your roadside-assistance number on paper; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 1 person: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and an allergy medicine): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 10 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, CDC, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 1 person and 14 days that is 3 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
1 bleeding-control kit: a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for serious bleeding, and a Stop the Bleed class so you know how to use them. Serious bleeding can kill before help arrives. (DHS)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. In a building, know both stairways and never use the elevator in a fire. Test your smoke alarms every month. (Ready.gov)

No carbon monoxide alarm yet: put one on every level where people sleep (1 for a home like yours), with battery backup. Replace them every 5 years or as the maker says. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

No fire extinguisher yet: 1 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguisher for a home on one floor, kept near the kitchen. Learn how to use it before you need it. Small home fires are common: CPSC estimated about 6.6 a year for every 100 households, most of them cooking fires, and fire departments attend only about 3 in 100 of them. (USFA, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)

You live on floor 2, above the ground: 1 escape ladder for a bedroom window, in case fire or smoke blocks the way out, unless every bedroom already has a second way out such as a fire escape. Keep it by the window and practise with it. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

N95 respirators, for about 5 days of smoke, dust or ash: 1 a day for each of the 1 person aged 13 and over = 5 respirators. A well-fitting N95 protects far more than a cloth or surgical mask; replace it when breathing through it gets harder. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter for your clean room: for a room of about 200 square feet, a clean air delivery rate (CADR) of at least 130 for smoke (EPA's sizing, more for high ceilings). Keep a spare filter, and avoid air cleaners that make ozone. (EPA; some amounts are estimates)

Cheaper than an air cleaner: a 20-inch box fan with a 20 by 20 inch MERV 13 filter taped to its intake side, which EPA calls a cost-effective way to cut smoke indoors. Use a newer fan with safety features, and do not leave it running while no one is home. (EPA)

A clean-room plan for smoky or dusty days: pick one room with few windows and doors where everyone can sleep, keep it closed, set the heating or cooling to recirculate (or turn off fans that pull in outside air), run the air cleaner there, and do not fry food, burn candles or vacuum on those days. (EPA, CDC)

Savings goal: about 7 months of expenses ($18,200 at $2,600 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 2 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

You earn your household's money: check whether your job offers disability insurance. About 1 in 4 workers who start at 20 become disabled before retirement age. NAIC's buyer's guide helps you work out how much cover is enough. (SSA, NAIC)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: Most homes in your county are outside the mapped high-risk flood zone, and that is where many uninsured floods happen: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings, and renters can buy cover for belongings only. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)

warnings.message: No backup power for a medical device by month 3.
warnings.why: A breathing machine or other powered device stops when the power goes out. Ask the device supplier which battery or backup works with it, and ask your power company about its medical-needs list.

warnings.message: No stored water beyond refilled bottles by month 3.
warnings.why: Refilled drink bottles are a good start, but they hold only a little. Water is the one supply you cannot go long without: a few gallons of bottled water or a water jug is the next step, and costs little.

warnings.why: The smallest kit that covers three days of water, light, warmth and medicine comes first and is complete by month 4; everything else follows in the usual order, and the whole plan takes until month 42. Beyond three years at this budget: cleanup gear for each teen and adult: P100 respirator, goggles, work gloves, extra shelf-stable food you already eat, portable jump starter for the car and escape ladder for upstairs bedrooms. A little more each month, or a less cautious setting, brings them closer.

para.t:
**For:** 1 adult  
**Where:** Maricopa County, Arizona (ZIP code 85008)  
**Home:** a rented apartment on floor 2, with city water, a heat pump and central air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions (the 1-in-100 setting), in the climate expected around 2050. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]
> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** one month of supplies. At your budget, the bare minimum (three days of water, light, warmth and medicine) is in place by month 4 (February 2027), and everything by month 42 (April 2030). Start with the free steps under Your plan.
### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 35 (20–70) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. Be ready to manage about 3 days at home with no power, and about 5 days with no tap water.
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 55 (30–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 10 days of food you normally eat, and 3 weeks of daily medicine on hand.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (10–40) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. Losing a paycheck is the longest disruption most households face. Aim for about 7 months of expenses in savings over time, apart from this supplies budget.

**What the plan assumes you already have:** a charged mobile phone, go-bag for each person, manual can opener, a cooking pot with a lid and three days of the food you normally eat. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.
Fill this in together, here or on the "Your family plan" screen. Keep a copy in each go-bag and one on the fridge: phones die.[2]

| Plan | Ours |
| --- | --- |
| Meeting place near home | __________ |
| Meeting place outside the neighborhood | __________ |
| Out-of-area contact | __________ |
| Work and school plans | __________ |
| Shelter spot at home | __________ |
| Shelter spot at work or school | __________ |
| Where we would go | __________ |
| First way out | __________ |
| Second way out | __________ |
| Neighbors who check on us | __________ |
| Water shut-off | __________ |
| Electrical panel | __________ |
| Roadside assistance | __________ |
| Lawyer | __________ |
**Our trusted circle:** people who agreed to help, and what they hold for us.
**Numbers we know by heart:** __________
### Leaving home

Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (10–25) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years. Warning can be as short as a few minutes (a home fire) or as long as 12 hours. For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for wildfires, 15 minutes. Plan to be away for about 2 days. Most evacuations last a few days, but after a home fire you could be away for 2 months or more.[3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]
### Staying in touch

**Four ways to reach each other.** Emergency planners call this a PACE plan: a primary way, an alternate, a contingency and an emergency way. Each one takes over when the one before it fails.[12] For a household it can be:

1. Primary: call.
2. Alternate: text. A text may get through when a call does not, and it saves battery.[13]
3. Contingency: everyone texts one out-of-state contact, who passes the news along.[13]
4. Emergency: go to the place you agreed to meet if you get separated.[13]
Cut out a card for each person's wallet or phone case.

> **Wallet card: person 1 (adult)**
>
> - Out-of-area contact: __________
> - Meet near home: __________
> - Meet outside the neighborhood: __________
> - Lawyer: __________
> - Trusted circle: __________
> - Know by heart: __________
> - Medical notes: __________
### Medicine

- 1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 21 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. For medicine the plan keeps at most a month on hand: agencies advise 7 days to two weeks (Red Cross, CDC, Florida), and a longer target is kept up with 60- to 90-day fills from your drug plan (Medicare).[4, 10, 11, 57, 58, 62, 63, 152, 168, 171, 172, 173, 174, 175]
### Antibiotics

- No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones.[28, 29, 176, 177]
### Powered medical devices

- Backup power for medical equipment: a CPAP uses about 170 Wh a night with the humidifier on (about 96 with it off). That is about 170 Wh a day × 3 days = 510 Wh. Keep spare batteries charged, and ask your utility about its list for customers who need power for medical equipment.[3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 14, 15, 16, 26, 101, 106, 107, 178]
- 1 spare battery for each powered medical device: ask the maker which battery fits and how long it runs, and keep it charged.[26, 178]
- 1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) to run the medical equipment through the outage. Your essential load (medical equipment and phones) is about 185 Wh a day, 560 Wh for 3 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 4.9 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. (some amounts are estimates)[3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 14, 15, 16, 106, 107, 143, 150, 178, 179]

- **Power plan for a medical device.** Ask your doctor or supplier how to keep the device running in an outage and how long its battery lasts, and ask your power company to put you on its list for priority restoration (Ready.gov). Keep batteries charged and know where you would go if the power stays off.[26, 100, 101]
### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[180] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[181] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[182] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[183]

### What to know and do
#### 1. Heat wave
Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in a ten-year stretch around 2050 (about 14 times a year).[3, 14, 15, 16]
**Includes:** a blackout during a heat wave.

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[17] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[18] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[18] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[17] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[19]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[17] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[18] Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot, red skin that may be dry or damp, a fast, strong pulse, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler, cool them with cool cloths or a cool bath, and give them nothing to drink.[20]
**How bad:** Serious (based on data).
#### 2. Dust storm
Nearly every household like yours will be caught in a dust storm that closes roads or fouls the air at home in the next ten years.[10, 14]

**What helps.** If dense dust is blowing across the road ahead, avoid driving into it. If it reaches you, pull off the pavement as far as you can, stop, turn off all your lights, set the parking brake and take your foot off the brake pedal.[21] If you cannot pull off, slow down, turn on your lights, sound the horn now and then, and follow the painted center line.[21]
**What to avoid.** Never stop in a lane of traffic. Do not leave your lights on once you are parked off the road: drivers behind may follow them and hit you.[21]
**How bad:** Serious (rough data).
#### 3. Medical emergency
Of 100 households like yours, about 99 will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.[22]
**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[23] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[24] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[25] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[26] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[27]
**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[28] Do not use expired medicines.[29]
**How bad:** Serious (based on data).
#### 4. Burst pipe or water leak
Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (7–16) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[10, 30]
**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[31, 32] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[31] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[32] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[31]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[32] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[31]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 5. House fire
Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a house fire, in their home or next door in the next ten years.[10, 11]
**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[33] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[34] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[34] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[34] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[34] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[35]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[34] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[34] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[34]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 6. Wildfire
Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–17) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[3, 6, 10]

**What helps.** Keep a zone at least 30 feet around your home clear of leaves, debris and anything that burns.[36] Know your evacuation zone and routes, and practice with your pets.[36] Store N95 masks for smoke. Pick a room you can close off from outside air, and run a portable air cleaner there.[36] N95 masks are not made to fit children, so for them the clean room is the protection.[37] A box fan with a MERV 13 filter makes a low-cost air cleaner.[38] If your heating and cooling system brings in fresh air, set it to recirculate.[36] Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[36]

**What to avoid.** Leave as soon as authorities tell you to, even if you cannot see flames.[36, 39] Do not use an air cleaner that makes ozone.[40] Avoid hard exercise when it is smoky, so you breathe in less smoke.[40]
**How bad:** Moderate (rough data).
#### 7. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (fewer than 1 to 5) will be cut off or lose building services in a flood in the next ten years.[9, 10]
**Includes:** flash flood; basement or street flooding in heavy rain.

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[41] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[41] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[42] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[41]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[41] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[43] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[41] Leave if you are told to.[44]
**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).
#### 8. Hail
Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 2) will have hail damage their home or car in the next ten years.[6, 10]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[45] In an apartment building, pick an inside hallway, stairwell or small room with no windows, as low in the building as you can get to quickly. Stay off the elevators.[46, 47] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[45] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[48]
**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[45] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[48]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

### After that
From month 2 the plan follows Checklists, free steps first; each line gives its month.
### When you are done
Every need is covered by month 42 (April 2030). After that, keep up the maintenance calendar and put the same money toward savings.
### Things to watch

- **Worth acting on: No backup power for a medical device by month 3.** A breathing machine or other powered device stops when the power goes out. Ask the device supplier which battery or backup works with it, and ask your power company about its medical-needs list.
- **Worth acting on: No stored water beyond refilled bottles by month 3.** Refilled drink bottles are a good start, but they hold only a little. Water is the one supply you cannot go long without: a few gallons of bottled water or a water jug is the next step, and costs little.
- **Worth acting on: At this budget the full plan would take more than three years, so it starts with the bare minimum.** The smallest kit that covers three days of water, light, warmth and medicine comes first and is complete by month 4; everything else follows in the usual order, and the whole plan takes until month 42. Beyond three years at this budget: cleanup gear for each teen and adult: P100 respirator, goggles, work gloves, extra shelf-stable food you already eat, portable jump starter for the car and escape ladder for upstairs bedrooms. A little more each month, or a less cautious setting, brings them closer.

pages.title: When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast

para.t: Hurricanes, winter storms and heat waves usually come with warning. Keep your phone charged when one is forecast, and use the time the same way each time.[139]
**Before any storm**

- Charge phones, power banks and other batteries.[141] 
- Fill the car's tank and get some cash, since card readers and cash machines need power.[141] Charge the power station.[141] If you would leave in an electric car, charge it fully.[142]
- Refill prescriptions if you can.[141]
- Fill the bathtub and other large containers with water for flushing and cleaning.[141]
- Turn the fridge to its coldest setting and keep the doors shut.[141] A full freezer keeps food cold for about 48 hours, a fridge for about four.[101]
- Bring in or tie down outdoor furniture and grills.[139]
- Check your evacuation zone and your plan to leave.[139]
- Check with neighbors, older adults and anyone who may need help.[139]

**Before a hard freeze.** Let hot and cold water drip from a faucet at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher. Make sure everyone knows how to shut off the water in case a pipe bursts.[32]

**Before a heat wave.** Pick a place to cool down, such as a library, or ask your local health department about cooling options. Plan to check on family, older adults and neighbors. Fans do not lower body temperature.[18]

pages.title: After a disaster: the first 30 days

para.t: **Your county.** Maricopa County, Arizona had no federal major-disaster declarations in the last five full years.[160]
Recovery takes weeks. These steps come in rough order.

**Going home.** Go back only when local officials say it is safe. Do not go inside if you smell gas or the building looks damaged.[161] Run a generator only outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[100]

**Insurance and records.** Before you clean up, take photos and videos and make a list of the damage.[161] Keep every receipt.[162] Call your insurer as soon as you can, and an adjuster will come to inspect. Check the adjuster's estimate, and talk to them before you sign a repair contract.[163]
**Help from FEMA.** If a federal disaster declaration covers your county, apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.[164] FEMA help does not replace insurance.[165]

**Scams.** FEMA never charges to apply or to inspect.[166] Its inspectors carry an official photo ID and never ask for your bank details; a FEMA shirt is not an ID.[162] Never sign your insurance check over to a contractor, and walk away from anyone who wants cash up front.[167]

**Medicine.** In a declared disaster, Medicare drug plans can help you find a pharmacy and replace lost medicine.[168] Many states let a pharmacist give an emergency supply when your prescriber cannot be reached, and the rules differ by state.[152] Healthcare Ready's Rx Open map shows which pharmacies are open in a disaster area.[169]
**Papers.** To replace lost IDs, start with your birth certificate, from the vital records office of the state where you were born.[170]

# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 1 adult  
**Where:** Maricopa County, Arizona (ZIP code 85008)  
**Home:** a rented apartment on floor 2, with city water, a heat pump and central air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions (the 1-in-100 setting), in the climate expected around 2050. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** one month of supplies. At your budget, the bare minimum (three days of water, light, warmth and medicine) is in place by month 4 (February 2027), and everything by month 42 (April 2030). ## Your risks

What could reach a household like yours in Maricopa County, Arizona over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first.

### What to know and do

#### 1. Heat wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in a ten-year stretch around 2050 (about 14 times a year).[3, 14, 15, 16]

**Includes:** a blackout during a heat wave.

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[17] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[18] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[18] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[17] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[19]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[17] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[18] Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot, red skin that may be dry or damp, a fast, strong pulse, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler, cool them with cool cloths or a cool bath, and give them nothing to drink.[20]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 2. Dust storm

Nearly every household like yours will be caught in a dust storm that closes roads or fouls the air at home in the next ten years.[10, 14]

**What helps.** If dense dust is blowing across the road ahead, avoid driving into it. If it reaches you, pull off the pavement as far as you can, stop, turn off all your lights, set the parking brake and take your foot off the brake pedal.[21] If you cannot pull off, slow down, turn on your lights, sound the horn now and then, and follow the painted center line.[21]

**What to avoid.** Never stop in a lane of traffic. Do not leave your lights on once you are parked off the road: drivers behind may follow them and hit you.[21]

**How bad:** Serious (rough data).

#### 3. Medical emergency

Of 100 households like yours, about 99 will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.[22]

**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[23] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[24] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[25] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[26] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[27]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[28] Do not use expired medicines.[29]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 4. Burst pipe or water leak

Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (7–16) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[10, 30]

**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[31, 32] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[31] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[32] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[31]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[32] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[31]

**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

#### 5. House fire

Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a house fire, in their home or next door in the next ten years.[10, 11]

**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[33] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[34] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[34] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[34] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[34] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[35]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[34] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[34] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[34]

**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

#### 6. Wildfire

Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–17) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[3, 6, 10]

**What helps.** Keep a zone at least 30 feet around your home clear of leaves, debris and anything that burns.[36] Know your evacuation zone and routes, and practice with your pets.[36] Store N95 masks for smoke. Pick a room you can close off from outside air, and run a portable air cleaner there.[36] N95 masks are not made to fit children, so for them the clean room is the protection.[37] A box fan with a MERV 13 filter makes a low-cost air cleaner.[38] If your heating and cooling system brings in fresh air, set it to recirculate.[36] Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[36]

**What to avoid.** Leave as soon as authorities tell you to, even if you cannot see flames.[36, 39] Do not use an air cleaner that makes ozone.[40] Avoid hard exercise when it is smoky, so you breathe in less smoke.[40]

**How bad:** Moderate (rough data).

#### 7. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain

Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (fewer than 1 to 5) will be cut off or lose building services in a flood in the next ten years.[9, 10]

**Includes:** flash flood; basement or street flooding in heavy rain.

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[41] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[41] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[42] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[41]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[41] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[43] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[41] Leave if you are told to.[44]

**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

#### 8. Hail

Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 2) will have hail damage their home or car in the next ten years.[6, 10]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[45] In an apartment building, pick an inside hallway, stairwell or small room with no windows, as low in the building as you can get to quickly. Stay off the elevators.[46, 47] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[45] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[48]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[45] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[48]

**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

### No grid power at home: about 3 days (2–7)

**What helps.** A light for each person, a radio and phone power are in your plan; keeping food cold and charging up are on the forecast list; registries are under Local help.

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[100] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[101] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911.[102] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[101] Treat every downed power line as live: stay at least 35 feet from it and anything it touches, and call 911.[103, 104] If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.[105]

The worst power cut in your region's records (where it was worst, about 102 miles (164 km) away) was winter storm, January 2023; being ready for 3 days would have outlasted it for at least 9 in 10 of the homes that lost power.[3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 14, 15, 16, 106, 107]

### Tap water must be treated: about 5 days (1 day to 2 weeks)

**What helps.** Use bottled water, or bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute. Boil for three minutes above 5,000 feet, then let it cool.[108] If you cannot boil water, add plain unscented bleach: 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon. Stir, and wait 30 minutes.[108] Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, baby formula and ice. If the power is out too, a camp stove works, but only outdoors.[100]

**What to avoid.** Do not use water or ice from the fridge dispenser while a notice is on. Boil tap water even if it went through a home filter or a filter pitcher.[109] Boiling does not help if the notice warns of chemicals. That is a do-not-drink notice, and you need stored or bottled water instead.[109, 110]

### No tap water at all: about 5 days (2–10)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[111] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[112] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[113, 114] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[98] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[110] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[115]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[111] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[116] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[114] After a flood, do not drink from a private well until it has been disinfected and tested. Your health department can tell you how.[117]

## Your shelter plan

Pick a spot for each danger below, at home and at work, and practice going there.[2]

**Strong wind.** In a high wind or severe thunderstorm warning, go inside a sturdy building, to an inside room.[137] Stay away from windows while damaging wind is near.[138]

**Hurricane.** If officials tell your evacuation zone to leave, go right away. If you stay, use an inside room away from windows.[139]

**Chemical release.** If told to stay inside, go to an above-ground room with few openings. Close the windows, doors and vents, turn off fans and air conditioning, and seal the room with plastic sheeting and duct tape.[140]

**Radiation.** If officials warn of fallout, get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Go to a basement or the middle of a brick or concrete building.[88]

## When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast

Hurricanes, winter storms and heat waves usually come with warning. Keep your phone charged when one is forecast, and use the time the same way each time.[139]

**Before any storm**

- Charge phones, power banks and other batteries.[141] 
- Fill the car's tank and get some cash, since card readers and cash machines need power.[141] Charge the power station.[141] If you would leave in an electric car, charge it fully.[142]
- Refill prescriptions if you can.[141]
- Fill the bathtub and other large containers with water for flushing and cleaning.[141]
- Turn the fridge to its coldest setting and keep the doors shut.[141] A full freezer keeps food cold for about 48 hours, a fridge for about four.[101]
- Bring in or tie down outdoor furniture and grills.[139]
- Check your evacuation zone and your plan to leave.[139]
- Check with neighbors, older adults and anyone who may need help.[139]

**Before a hard freeze.** Let hot and cold water drip from a faucet at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher. Make sure everyone knows how to shut off the water in case a pipe bursts.[32]

**Before a heat wave.** Pick a place to cool down, such as a library, or ask your local health department about cooling options. Plan to check on family, older adults and neighbors. Fans do not lower body temperature.[18]

## Documents and money

Keep paper copies in a waterproof pouch and photos you can reach from any phone. FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit groups them in four parts.[35]

- [ ] **Who you are:** photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, and pet records.
- [ ] **Money and legal papers:** insurance policies, the lease or deed, a will and powers of attorney, bank and card contact numbers (not PINs), and recent tax returns.
- [ ] **Medical papers:** insurance cards, the written medicine list, prescriptions, and vaccination records.
- [ ] **Contacts:** family, doctors, the insurance agent, the landlord or lender, and employers.

### Decisions

- [ ] **Decide: ID for every person (passport book or card, or a state ID).** A passport book or card for each person, children included, proves who you are and your citizenship if other papers are lost, and the card shows no home address; get them before you need them. The federal fee schedule: a first adult book $165 and card $65 ($130 and $30 plus a $35 acceptance fee), for children under 16 a book $135 and card $50 (22 CFR 22.1).[35, 153, 154]
- [ ] **Decide: flood insurance, even outside a flood zone.** Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: Most homes in your county are outside the mapped high-risk flood zone, and that is where many uninsured floods happen: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings, and renters can buy cover for belongings only.[9, 42, 155, 156, 157]
- [ ] **Decide: disability and life insurance for the people who earn.** You earn your household's money: check whether your job offers disability insurance. About 1 in 4 workers who start at 20 become disabled before retirement age. NAIC's buyer's guide helps you work out how much cover is enough.[64, 158]
